html:
The global order is significantly shaped today by escalating tensions between the United States and Iran, particularly concerning maritime security in the Strait of Hormuz, even as negotiations for a lasting ceasefire continue amidst heightened rhetoric and new US sanctions. This precarious situation threatens global energy markets and prompts international diplomatic efforts to de-escalate.

US-Iran Conflict: A shaky ceasefire between the U.S. and Iran appears to have paused, with the U.S. giving Iran a Saturday deadline to publicly declare the Strait of Hormuz open for all and pledge to stop shooting at ships. Vice-President JD Vance is involved in ongoing negotiations in Oman, while Trump has reiterated the ceasefire is "over" but talks will continue, threatening to "decimate" Iran if it attempts to kill him and stating 1,000 missiles are ready. Privately, Iran told Trump advisers "they made a mistake" in shooting at ships, yet traffic in the Strait has sharply decreased, and the U.S. has issued fresh sanctions. Iranian diplomat Araghchi is in Oman for talks, emphasizing reciprocal compliance.

Ukraine Conflict: Ukrainian drones have struck southern Russian refineries and the port of Azov, contributing to a severe gasoline crisis in Russia, which has also banned diesel exports. Meanwhile, Trump has signaled support for letting Ukraine produce Patriot air defense missiles, a move welcomed by analysts as a sign of support, though production could take years. Russian advances are also reported on the outskirts of Zaporizhzhia.

Geopolitical Shifts: A NATO summit in Ankara saw Trump questioning the alliance's loyalty before leaving in a "markedly warmer mood," with attention on his relationship with Zelensky and support for Ukraine. Reports suggest Trump's team adjusted plans due to an ongoing Iranian assassination threat during the summit. In Iran, public mourning for its late Supreme Leader has concluded, and Mojtaba Khamenei, referred to as Iran's new supreme leader, has inherited the political system.

Middle East Security: A U.S. military delegation is in Beirut to help implement the Lebanon-Israel agreement, while Israeli strikes in southern Lebanon killed one person, violating an April ceasefire, with the Lebanese Health Ministry reporting 4,321 deaths since March 2, 2026, due to Israeli military attacks. Israel now controls nearly 70% of Gaza, pushing deeper since last year's ceasefire. The Jerusalem Grand Mufti has been banned from Al-Aqsa Mosque for a week, and EU countries are discussing a trade ban on illegal Israeli settlements.

Global Crises: Venezuela is grappling with a devastating earthquake, with the death toll surpassing 4,000 and nearly 17,000 injured, prompting calls for financial aid. Cuba has suffered its second nationwide blackout in five days amid a six-month U.S. fuel blockade imposed by Trump and dilapidated energy infrastructure. Additionally, Iran's economic pain is deepening, with paychecks barely covering food, as factions trade blame and new U.S. sanctions target an Iranian businessman.

Other Global Events: Meta has pulled its new AI image feature after days of backlash following its release, while Apple has sued OpenAI, its employees, claiming theft of trade secrets. In Canada, fears of a "Brexit-style upset" loom over an October vote on Alberta's future, with Canadian unity taking center stage at the Calgary Stampede. Separately, the Trump administration repealed a crucial part of the Endangered Species Act, opening imperiled wildlife habitats to development.
